subject: math
title: Grade 1 Equal and Not Equal
seo_title: Grade 1 Equal and Not Equal Worksheets (= and ≠): Free Math with Answer Key (Ontario Curriculum)
standard_text: Determine whether given pairs of addition and subtraction expressions are equivalent or not
meta_desc: Free Grade 1 math worksheets on equal and not equal for the Ontario curriculum: balances, the = and ≠ signs, is 3 + 4 the same as 5 + 2, missing numbers like 6 + 2 = □ + 3, and things that change or stay the same. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: The = sign means “is the same as.” The ≠ sign means “is not equal to.”
key_sub: 3 + 4 = 5 + 2 because both sides are 7. 4 + 4 ≠ 5 + 2 because 8 is not 7. In 6 + 2 = □ + 3, the box is 5, not 8.
body_html:
= means “the same as”

The = sign means is the same as. Both sides must have the same amount. It does not mean “the answer comes next.” Think of a balance. When both sides are the same, it is level.

≠ means “is not equal to”

When the two sides are not the same, use ≠. The heavier side of the balance goes down.

Two sidesLeftRightSign
3 + 4 and 5 + 277=
4 + 4 and 5 + 287≠
9 − 2 and 4 + 377=
20 + 5 and 10 + 152525=

Find the missing number

A box □ is a number you do not know. Find the side you know first. Then make the other side the same.

Example

6 + 2 = □ + 3

The left side is 6 + 2 = 8. Now □ + 3 = 8. Count up from 3: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. That is 5.

Answer: 5

Example

20 + 5 = 10 + □

The left side is 25. 10 + 15 = 25.

Answer: 15

What changes and what stays the same?

Some things change. Your age goes up every year. A plant gets taller. Some things stay the same. Your birthday is the same date every year. A week always has 7 days. If you move 8 beads around, you still have 8.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
6 + 2 = □ + 3, so □ = 88 is the left side. □ + 3 = 8, so □ = 5
6 + 2 = □ + 3, so □ = 11 (adding all)Make both sides the same, do not add everything
3 + 4 and 5 + 2 are not equal because the numbers are differentFind each side: both are 7, so they are equal
7 = 8 − 1 is wrong because the answer is firstThe = sign can come first. Both sides are 7
30 + 5 = 830 is 3 tens, not 3. 30 + 5 = 35

faq.q: What does the not equal sign (≠) mean in Grade 1 math?
faq.a: The ≠ sign means “is not equal to.” For example, 4 + 4 ≠ 5 + 2 because 8 is not the same as 7.

faq.q: How do you teach the equal sign in Grade 1?
faq.a: Use a pan balance: when both sides have the same amount, it is level. This shows that = means “is the same as,” not “the answer comes next,” so 3 + 4 = 5 + 2 is true.
Find the side you know first: 6 + 2 = 8. Then ask what number plus 3 makes 8. Count up from 3 to 8, so the box is 5, not 8.

faq.q: What does “quantities that change and stay the same” mean in the Ontario Grade 1 curriculum?
faq.a: In the Algebra strand (C2.1), students notice that some amounts change, like your age or a plant’s height, while others stay the same, like your birthday or the 7 days in a week.

sets.title: Find the missing number to balance

items.q:
What number makes it balance?
6 + 2 = □ + 3
items.e: The side you know is 6 + 2 = 8. The other side must be 8 too. □ + 3 = 8. Count up from 3 to 8: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. That is 5. So □ = 5. Not 8: the answer does not come right after =.

items.q:
What number makes it balance?
4 + 3 = □ + 5
items.e: The side you know is 4 + 3 = 7. The other side must be 7 too. □ + 5 = 7. Count up from 5 to 7: 6, 7. That is 2. So □ = 2. Not 7: the answer does not come right after =.

items.q:

items.e: The side you know is 5 + 5 = 10. The other side must be 10 too. □ + 6 = 10. Count up from 6 to 10: 7, 8, 9, 10. That is 4. So □ = 4. Not 10: the answer does not come right after =.

items.q:

items.e: The side you know is 3 + 6 = 9. The other side must be 9 too. 2 + □ = 9. Think: 2 + 7 = 9. So □ = 7. Not 9: the answer does not come right after =.

sets.title: Same or not the same? Word problems

items.q: Olivia is 6 today. What will change next year?
items.e: Next year Olivia will be 7. Her age changes every year. Her birthday is the same date every year.

items.q: Ethan turns 7 on May 12. What stays the same every year?
items.e: His birthday is May 12 every year. His age, height and shoe size change as he grows.

items.q: A week has 7 days. Does that change?
items.e: Every week has 7 days, from Sunday to Saturday. That always stays the same.

items.q: Look at the plant. What changes?
items.e: The plant gets taller in May, June and July. How tall it is changes. The pot stays the same.

items.q: Priya has 5 red beads and 3 blue beads. She moves them around. How many beads now?
items.e: 5 + 3 = 8. Moving the beads does not change how many there are. Priya still has 8 beads.

items.q: Jayden is 6 years old. How old will he be next year?
items.e: Your age goes up by 1 each year. 6 + 1 = 7. Not 6: age changes.

items.q: Nathan has 4 red mitts and 3 blue mitts. Hana has 7 mitts. Do they have the same number?
items.e: Nathan: 4 + 3 = 7. Hana: 7. 4 + 3 = 7, so yes.

items.q: Maya has 5 hockey cards. She gets 3 more. Benjamin has 9. Do they have the same number?
c: Yes. They have the same cards.
items.e: Maya: 5 + 3 = 8. Benjamin: 9. 8 is not 9, so no: 5 + 3 ≠ 9.

items.q: 5 kids skate at the rink. 3 more come. 4 kids sled on the hill. 4 more come. Same number at the rink and the hill?
items.e: Rink: 5 + 3 = 8. Hill: 4 + 4 = 8. Both are 8, so yes: 5 + 3 = 4 + 4.

items.q: Liam has 10 maple leaves. He gives 3 away. Olivia has 9 leaves. She gives 2 away. Do they have the same number now?
items.e: Liam: 10 − 3 = 7. Olivia: 9 − 2 = 7. Both have 7, so yes: 10 − 3 = 9 − 2.

items.q: Priya has 6 apples and 2 pears. Jayden has 3 apples. How many pears must he get to have the same?
items.e: Priya has 6 + 2 = 8. Jayden needs 8 too. 3 + □ = 8. Count up from 3 to 8: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. That is 5. So he needs 5 pears. Not 8: that is Priya’s total.

items.q: Emma has 4 red crayons and 5 blue crayons. Nathan has 9 crayons. Which number sentence fits?
items.e: Emma has 4 + 5. Nathan has 9. 4 + 5 = 9, so they are the same: 4 + 5 = 9.

items.q: Hana has 2 boxes of 10 crayons and 5 more. Noah has 25 crayons. Do they have the same number?
items.e: Hana: 10 + 10 + 5 = 25. Noah: 25. Both have 25, so yes. Not 7: each box is 10, not 1.

items.q: Maya has 30 stickers. Benjamin has 10 + 10 + 5. How many more does he need to have the same?
items.e: Benjamin has 10 + 10 + 5 = 25. Maya has 30. 25 + 5 = 30, so 5 more. Not 25: that is how many he has now.

items.q: In the Terry Fox Run, Room 1 has 6 girls and 4 boys. Room 2 has 3 girls and some boys. Both rooms have the same number. How many boys are in Room 2?
items.e: Room 1: 6 + 4 = 10. Room 2 must have 10 too. 3 + □ = 10. 3 + 7 = 10, so 7 boys. Not 10: that is all of Room 1.

items.q: The class needs 20 apples for a field trip. Ava brings 12. Liam brings 6. Is that 20 apples?
items.e: 12 + 6 = 18. 18 is not 20, so no: 12 + 6 ≠ 20. They need 2 more.

items.q: A tower has 7 blue blocks and 5 red blocks. Another has 10 green blocks. How many green blocks must you add to make them the same?
items.e: 7 + 5 = 12. 10 + □ = 12. 10 + 2 = 12, so add 2 blocks. Not 12: that is the first tower.

items.q: For Thanksgiving, Grandma makes 9 pumpkin tarts and 6 apple tarts. Lucas makes 10 tarts. How many more tarts must he make to have the same?
items.e: Grandma: 9 + 6 = 15. Lucas: 10 + □ = 15. 10 + 5 = 15, so 5 tarts. Not 15: that is Grandma’s total.

items.q: Ethan has 8 cards. He gives 3 away. Priya has 2 cards. She gets 3 more. They have the same. Which number sentence fits?
At the cottage, Canoe A has 4 kids and 4 adults. Canoe B has 6 kids and some adults. Both canoes have the same number of people. How many adults are in Canoe B?
items.e: Canoe A: 4 + 4 = 8. Canoe B: 6 + □ = 8. 6 + 2 = 8, so 2 adults. Not 8: that is everyone in Canoe A.
